paras.html: Jurisdiction over "application or operation": Under Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII, the Court en banc hears cases involving the constitutionality, application or operation of "other regulations" such as PNP CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112. It may therefore require the production of police reports on how they were implemented, but only to determine the reports' existence, whether they were prepared as mandated, and whether they facially show compliance — not the veracity of their contents, since the Court is not a trier of facts.

paras.html: Relevance is for the Court to determine: Whether evidence is relevant rests largely in the Court's discretion, exercised according to logic and everyday experience (Sec. 4, Rule 128); a party cannot arrogate that determination to itself.

paras.html: No blanket national-security or regularity shield: Records of routine police operations against illegal drugs are not state secrets; the presumption of regularity does not attach because deaths are not supposed to occur in police operations; and willful suppression of the records will lead the Court to presume they are adverse (Sec. 3(e), Rule 131).

paras.html: 17 November 2017 – Advisory. The Court framed the issues: (1) the constitutionality of CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112, including their legal basis and whether they direct any unlawful act; (2) whether the acts authorized or conducted under them violate Art. II, Sec. 11 and Art. III, Secs. 1, 2, 12, 14, and 17 of the Constitution, RA 7438, the buy-bust and stop-and-frisk case law, Art. 125 RPC, PNP operational procedures, and DOJ Circular No. 61; (3) whether they violate international obligations (ICCPR, Minnesota Protocol); and (4) whether the writ of amparo ought to issue, plus procedural sub-issues (class suit, standing, jurisdiction, joinder, verification).

paras.html: J. Carpio: The SG said 3,806 were killed in "legitimate" drug operations since 1 July 2016 and about 4,000 fall under "deaths under investigation" (DUI). He said 419 Chinese nationals were arrested (a mix of users, pushers, and drug lords) and that drug users rose from 1.8 million (2015, per the CMC) to about 4 million, conceding the earlier figure was "understated." Carpio asked why the campaign targets street-level pushers rather than the bulk smugglers the CMC itself identifies.

paras.html: J. Martires: The SG read the Almora spot report (Baguio City, 28 July 2016; joint operation of several PNP units; suspect "upon sensing" he was dealing with police allegedly shot first and died; four sachets of suspected shabu recovered). The SG added the operation targeted the "Lakay group."

paras.html: 5 December 2017 – Resolution. The Court directed the SG to submit, for police drug operations and for DUIs from 1 July 2016 to 30 November 2017: the place, date, and time; the PNP team; pre-operation plans; whether warrants were issued; the media, NGO, and barangay representatives present; the names, addresses, genders, and ages of those killed; post-operation reports; the DUI investigators, investigation reports, and charges filed; and, for the Daño petition, the list of San Andres Bukid buy-busts since Tokhang began and the pre- and post-operation reports of the 25 fatal buy-busts. Memoranda and documents were due in 30 days, extended to 60 days on the SG's motion because of their volume.

paras.html: Sec. 4, Rule 128: evidence must have such relation to the fact in issue as to induce belief in its existence or non-existence. There is no precise universal test; relevancy is determined by logic and human experience and rests largely in the court's discretion (People v. Galleno). Evidence is relevant if it tends "in any reasonable degree" to establish the probability or improbability of a fact in issue.

paras.html: Prior concurrence of the Monetary Board (Sec. 20, Art. VII): The requirement is not read literally as full MB approval before the loan is signed. It is “enabled through a more detailed and elaborate procedure”: an Approval-in-Principle before negotiations, signing subject to its conditions, and a Final Approval after signing but before the borrower may draw on the loan. Only the Approval-in-Principle is, strictly speaking, prior action, but the MB's participation does not end there.
paras.text: Prior concurrence of the Monetary Board (Sec. 20, Art. VII): The requirement is not read literally as full MB approval before the loan is signed. It is “enabled through a more detailed and elaborate procedure”: an Approval-in-Principle before negotiations, signing subject to its conditions, and a Final Approval after signing but before the borrower may draw on the loan. Only the Approval-in-Principle is, strictly speaking, prior action, but the MB's participation does not end there.

paras.html: Public information on foreign loans (Sec. 21, Art. XII): “Shall be made available to the public” is proactive and unqualified. A confidentiality clause that keeps all terms secret, requires the lender's prior consent, and allows disclosure only to government bodies cannot, for future purposes, withstand constitutional scrutiny (pronounced as guidance; the disclosure issue was moot).

paras.html: Filipino First Policy and foreign-funded procurement: Foreign loan arrangements that are executive agreements may adopt their own (hybrid) procurement rules despite deviating from RA 9184, but pacta sunt servanda cannot override the Constitution: bidding rules for such projects “must give preference, or at least equal opportunity, to qualified Filipinos.” The Filipino First Policy is not a Filipino monopoly.

paras.html: October 20, 2016: The GRP, through the DOF, and the Chinese government-owned Export-Import Bank of China (EXIM Bank) signed a Memorandum of Understanding on Financing Cooperation (MOU). Under Arts. 1.1, 2.3, 4.1, and 4.2, the MOU was a precursor to more binding and detailed loan agreements for GRP-nominated priority infrastructure projects; it was not legally binding except Arts. 3 to 7, and each loan agreement's terms were left to further negotiation.

paras.html: (1) the DOF requests concessional loan financing for priority projects through the PRC Embassy; (2) the Chinese Government gives its considerations and a list of at least three qualified, legitimate, and reputable Chinese contractors; (3) the implementing agency (IA) conducts Limited Competitive Bidding (LCB) among them and signs the commercial contract; (4) the DOF submits documents to EXIM Bank for due diligence; and (5) the DOF and EXIM Bank sign the loan agreement (and guarantee agreement, if any).

paras.html: A mutually agreed Clarificatory Procedures (DOF letter dated June 29, 2017) added that the IA shall adhere to RA 9184 (GPRA), conduct its own due diligence and vetting of the listed firms (coursing concerns through the DOF to the PRC Embassy), undertake LCB incorporating some GPRA procedures, and sign a contract whose effectivity is contingent on the effectivity of the loan agreement.

paras.html: Unlike the U.S. version, Philippine immunity does not distinguish official from personal acts or turn on the nature of the suit. Rationale: free the President from hindrance or distraction (Soliven v. Makasiar); protect the dignity of the office (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo). The President need not personally invoke it first.

paras.html: Scope of the foreign borrowing power: The power to contract or guarantee foreign loans under Sec. 20, Art. VII is construed broadly. The Constitution "makes no prohibition on the issuance of certain kinds of loans or distinctions as to which kinds of debt instruments are more onerous than others." Bond conversion (a bond is a loan) and debt buyback (a necessary implied power of the borrowing power) are within it. The only restrictions are the prior concurrence of the Monetary Board and such limitations as may be provided under law (e.g., RA 245, as amended by PD 142).
paras.text: Scope of the foreign borrowing power: The power to contract or guarantee foreign loans under Sec. 20, Art. VII is construed broadly. The Constitution "makes no prohibition on the issuance of certain kinds of loans or distinctions as to which kinds of debt instruments are more onerous than others." Bond conversion (a bond is a loan) and debt buyback (a necessary implied power of the borrowing power) are within it. The only restrictions are the prior concurrence of the Monetary Board and such limitations as may be provided under law (e.g., RA 245, as amended by PD 142).

paras.html: Exercise by alter ego: Under the doctrine of qualified political agency, the Secretary of Finance may exercise the foreign borrowing power as the President's alter ego. It does not belong to the exceptional class of powers that the President must exercise in person (declaring martial law, suspending the privilege of the writ, pardoning). However, the alter ego must secure the President's prior consent or subsequent ratification, and the President's repudiation of the alter ego's acts is binding.

paras.html: Limits of judicial review: The Art. II state policies are "not a panacea that can annul every governmental act." That petitioners prefer another debt-relief approach goes into the wisdom of the executive act, which courts do not review; the assailed acts enjoy a strong presumption of validity.

paras.html: On 28 February 1992, the Philippine Debt Negotiating Team, chaired by respondent Pelaez, negotiated with the country's Bank Advisory Committee (representing all foreign commercial bank creditors) the Philippine Comprehensive Financing Program for 1992, which respondents called "a multi-option financing package." paras.html: Option 2: conversion of existing debt instruments into bonds/securities: (a) new money bonds with a five-year grace period and 17-year final maturity, the purchase of which would let creditors convert eligible debt papers into bearer bonds with the same terms; (b) interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity; and (c) principal-collateralized interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity.

paras.html: Villena v. Secretary of the Interior (adopted from American jurisprudence): the Constitution establishes a single, not plural, Executive. United States), "each head of a department is, and must be, the President's alter ego in the matters of that department where the President is required by law to exercise authority."

paras.html: Declaring a national emergency vs. exercising emergency powers: The President alone may declare a state of national emergency (Sec. 18, Art. VII), even without a congressional enactment. But "the exercise of emergency powers, such as the taking over of privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest, is a different matter. This requires a delegation from Congress." Sec. 17, Art. XII is read in pari materia with Sec. 23(2), Art. VI, so the "State" in Sec. 17, Art. XII refers to Congress.

This requires a delegation from Congress." Sec. 17, Art. XII is read in pari materia with Sec. 23(2), Art. VI, so the "State" in Sec. 17, Art. XII refers to Congress.

paras.html: The calling-out power is the most benign power and is not martial law: PP 1017 is constitutional only insofar as it calls on the AFP to prevent or suppress lawless violence. The President "cannot invoke a greater power when he wishes to act under a lesser power"; the calling-out power cannot justify warrantless arrests, bans on assemblies, media takeovers or censorship, or the issuance of decrees.

paras.html: Review of the calling-out power: The Court may examine whether the power was exercised within constitutional limits or with grave abuse of discretion, but the standard is arbitrariness, not correctness, and the petitioner must show that the President's decision is "totally bereft of factual basis."

paras.html: On February 24, 2006, as the nation celebrated the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued Proclamation No. 1017 (PP 1017) declaring a state of national emergency. Its operative portion reads:
paras.text: On February 24, 2006, as the nation celebrated the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued Proclamation No. 1017 (PP 1017) declaring a state of national emergency. Its operative portion reads:

paras.html: "…by virtue of the powers vested upon me by Section 18, Article 7 of the Philippine Constitution… and in my capacity as their Commander-in-Chief, do hereby command the Armed Forces of the Philippines, to maintain law and order throughout the Philippines, prevent or suppress all forms of lawless violence as well as any act of insurrection or rebellion and to enforce obedience to all the laws and to all decrees, orders and regulations promulgated by me personally or upon my direction; and as provided in Section 17, Article 12 of the Constitution do hereby declare a State of National Emergency."
paras.text: "…by virtue of the powers vested upon me by Section 18, Article 7 of the Philippine Constitution… and in my capacity as their Commander-in-Chief, do hereby command the Armed Forces of the Philippines, to maintain law and order throughout the Philippines, prevent or suppress all forms of lawless violence as well as any act of insurrection or rebellion and to enforce obedience to all the laws and to all decrees, orders and regulations promulgated by me personally or upon my direction; and as provided in Section 17, Article 12 of the Constitution do hereby declare a State of National Emergency."

paras.html: The WHEREAS clauses cited a "tactical alliance" among elements of the political opposition, the extreme Left (NDF-CPP-NPA), and the extreme Right (military adventurists) to bring down the government; claims "recklessly magnified by certain segments of the national media"; harm to the economy; and a "clear and present danger" to the State.

paras.html: On the same day, the President issued General Order No. 5 (G.O. No. 5) implementing PP 1017. It called upon the AFP and the PNP "to prevent and suppress acts of terrorism and lawless violence in the country," and directed them "to immediately carry out the necessary and appropriate actions and measures to suppress and prevent acts of terrorism and lawless violence."

paras.html: Re: Standing in public suits
paras.text: Re: Standing in public suits

paras.html: Locus standi is "a right of appearance in a court of justice on a given question." Private suits follow the real-party-in-interest rule (Sec. 2, Rule 3). In public suits, the plaintiff sues as a representative of the public (as a "citizen" or "taxpayer") and must show sufficient interest in vindicating the public order.

In public suits, the plaintiff sues as a representative of the public (as a "citizen" or "taxpayer") and must show sufficient interest in vindicating the public order.

paras.html: Beauchamp v. Silk distinguished the taxpayer (affected by expenditure of public funds) from the citizen ("mere instrument of the public concern").

paras.html: The stricter "direct injury" test (Ex Parte Levitt; Tileston v. Ullman) was adopted in People v. Vera: the challenger must have "a personal and substantial interest in the case such that he has sustained, or will sustain direct injury as a result."

paras.html: Being a mere procedural technicality, standing may be waived for "transcendental importance": Araneta v. Dinglasan (1949 Emergency Powers Cases), Aquino v. Comelec, Chavez v. PEA, BAYAN v. Zamora, and Lim v. Executive Secretary.

paras.html: Summary of rules: taxpayers, voters, concerned citizens, and legislators may sue if (1) the case involves constitutional issues; (2) taxpayers claim illegal disbursement of public funds or an unconstitutional tax measure; (3) voters show obvious interest in the validity of the election law; (4) concerned citizens show that the issues are of transcendental importance and must be settled early; and (5) legislators claim that the act infringes their prerogatives as legislators.

paras.html: Re: Backdrop — political theorists on emergency power
paras.text: Re: Backdrop — political theorists on emergency power

paras.html: Locke (prerogative; the only remedy against abuse is "to appeal to Heaven"), Rousseau (temporary "supreme magistracy" of limited tenure), Mill (temporary dictatorship in extreme necessity), Machiavelli (standby emergency powers built into the constitution, with checks), and the "constitutional dictatorship" theorists Watkins, Friedrich, and Rossiter (e.g., the dictator should not decide when the emergency exists or ends).

paras.html: Scott and Cotter rejected "constitutional dictatorship" in favor of McIlwain's "constitutionalism": government should be limited, not weak; its two elements are legal limits to arbitrary power and political responsibility to the governed.

paras.html: The 1987 Constitution follows Justice Jackson's "balanced power structure" (Youngstown): each branch is supreme in its sphere, but none has a monopoly of power in times of emergency. In emergencies, the Constitution reposes faith in the Chief Executive but obliges him to operate within carefully prescribed procedural limitations.

paras.html: First, overbreadth is an analytical tool for testing statutes on their faces in free speech cases (US "First Amendment" cases). PP 1017 is not primarily directed at speech; it is a call on the AFP to suppress lawless violence, which is harmful, constitutionally unprotected conduct (U.S. v. Salerno; Broadrick v. Oklahoma).

paras.html: Second, facial invalidation is "manifestly strong medicine", used sparingly and only as a last resort. Ordinarily a litigant cannot challenge a law on the ground that it may conceivably be applied unconstitutionally to others; overbreadth departs from that rule only because of the chilling effect on third parties' speech (Younger v. Harris).

paras.html: Re 4.2: First provision — the calling-out power (Sec. 18, Art. VII) — VALID; NOT martial law
paras.text: Re 4.2: First provision — the calling-out power (Sec. 18, Art. VII) — VALID; NOT martial law

paras.html: Sanlakas: Sec. 18, Art. VII grants the President a "sequence" of graduated powers, from the most to the least benign: the calling-out power, suspension of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus, and martial law. Citing IBP v. Zamora, the only criterion for calling out is "whenever it becomes necessary" to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion, or rebellion. Owing to her vast intelligence network, the President is in the best position to determine that necessity.

paras.html: The calling-out power involves ordinary police action. Every act beyond it is ultra vires: "He cannot invoke a greater power when he wishes to act under a lesser power… the greater the power, the greater are the limitations."

paras.html: Distinguished from Sanlakas: the "state of rebellion" there rested on the President's power as Chief Executive and on Sec. 4, Ch. 2, Book II [sic: Book III] of the Administrative Code (proclamations declaring "a status or condition of public moment"), so it was "harmless, without legal significance, and deemed not written." PP 1017 is more than that: it also invokes Sec. 17, Art. XII, an "awesome power" to take over private businesses, so it cannot be deemed harmless.

Mendoza (retired Justice) before the Senate Committee on Justice on March 13, 2006: martial law is the most severe threat to civil liberties and "strong medicine"; PP 1017 is no more than a call to the armed forces; and (a) warrantless arrests and seizures, (b) bans on public assemblies, (c) take-over of news media and press censorship, and (d) issuance of Presidential Decrees can be exercised by the Commander-in-Chief only under a valid declaration of martial law or suspension of the writ.

paras.html: Since she cannot enact decrees, they are void and cannot be enforced. paras.html: Sec. 17, Art. XII: "In times of national emergency, when the public interest so requires, the State may, during the emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, temporarily take over or direct the operation of any privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest."

paras.html: Why invoke it? PP 1017 purports to grant the President, without authority or delegation from Congress, the power to take over or direct private public utilities and businesses. The provision was first introduced in the 1973 Constitution, a product of the "martial law" thinking of the 1971 ConCon; Marcos's LOI No. 2 (1972) had the SND take over Meralco, PLDT, NAWASA, PNR, PAL, and others.

paras.html: (a) Declaring a state of national emergency — VALID. Sec. 18, Art. VII grants the President this power, so no legitimate objection arises. Sec. 23(2), Art. VI speaks of "war or other national emergency," but if the Framers meant to withhold the declaration of national emergency from the President and give it to Congress (as with the declaration of a state of war under Sec. 23(1)), they would have said so. → The President could validly declare a state of national emergency even without a congressional enactment.

paras.html: Provisions in pari materia are construed together. Sec. 17, Art. XII and Sec. 23(2), Art. VI both relate to national emergencies.

paras.html: Generally, Congress is the repository of emergency powers; Sec. 23(2) authorizes it to delegate them, and "a body cannot delegate a power not reposed upon it." Conditions for the delegation: (1) a war or other emergency; (2) a limited period only; (3) subject to restrictions Congress prescribes; and (4) exercised to carry out a national policy declared by Congress.

XII is an aspect of the emergency powers clause; the takeover is "just another facet" of emergency powers generally reposed in Congress. → When Sec. 17 says "the State may… under reasonable terms prescribed by it," it refers to Congress, not the President. Whether the President may exercise it depends on a law delegating it and prescribing reasonable terms.

Sawyer: the US President's seizure of steel mills could not be sustained under the Commander-in-Chief power or the executive power; seizing private property to keep labor disputes from stopping production "is a job for the Nation's lawmakers, not for its military authorities"; the take-care power "refutes the idea that he is to be a lawmaker."

paras.html: Meaning of "emergency": Cacho-Olivares's view (tsunamis, typhoons) is too limited. "Emergency" connotes conditions suddenly intensifying the danger to life or well-being beyond what is normal, with elements of intensity, variety, and perception. In the US since 1933, emergencies have been economic, natural disaster, and national security. Under our Constitution, it may include rebellion, economic crisis, pestilence or epidemic, typhoon, flood, or other similar catastrophe of nationwide proportions.

Without legislation, the President cannot (1) decide whether exceptional circumstances warrant a takeover, (2) determine when they have ceased, or (3) identify the businesses to be taken over. She has "no absolute authority to exercise all the powers of the State under Section 17, Article VII [sic: Art. XII] in the absence of an emergency powers act passed by Congress."

paras.html: Re 4.5: As-applied challenge
paras.text: Re 4.5: As-applied challenge

paras.html: Of the seven petitions, three show direct injury: David and Llamas (arrest), Cacho-Olivares/Tribune (raid), and KMU/NAFLU-KMU (dispersal). These injuries resulted from the implementation of PP 1017 pursuant to G.O. No. 5.

paras.html: PP 1017 is not invalidated by abusive implementation. Courts cannot declare statutes invalid merely because they may be abused; validity is judged by the general purpose and efficiency to accomplish the end desired, not by effects in a particular case. Nothing in PP 1017 allows the police, expressly or impliedly, to make illegal arrests or searches. Otherwise, given police blunders, "majority of the provisions of the Revised Penal Code would have been declared unconstitutional a long time ago."

paras.html: G.O. No. 5 is valid, except "acts of terrorism." General orders are "acts and commands of the President in his capacity as Commander-in-Chief," internal rules to subordinates that must be reasonable. G.O. No. 5 provides a valid standard: only "necessary and appropriate actions and measures" to suppress lawless violence.

paras.html: But unlike "lawless violence" (found in statutes and the Constitution), "acts of terrorism" is an amorphous, vague concept; Congress has yet to define and punish it. The international community also lacks an agreed definition ("One country's terrorist is another country's freedom fighter"). The word appears only in PD 1835, repealed by EO 167, and neither defines it.

paras.html: Without a definition, "it is President Arroyo alone… who has the discretion to determine what acts constitute terrorism", which may lead to indiscriminate warrantless arrests, raids, media takeovers, and dispersal of unfriendly assemblies (e.g., arresting people on a drinking spree as terrorists). These go beyond the calling-out power and violate the due process clause → the "acts of terrorism" portion of G.O. No. 5 is unconstitutional and deemed deleted.

paras.html: Sec. 2, Art. III: searches and arrests are normally unreasonable without a warrant. Neither exception in Sec. 5(a) or (b), Rule 113 applies: the arresting officers could only cite rallyists wearing "Oust Gloria Now" shirts and an erroneous belief that David led the rally. The inquest prosecutor released him; David was not even wearing the shirt, and wearing it would not suffice for inciting to sedition.

paras.html: Right to assembly (Sec. 4, Art. III): not to be limited except on a showing of clear and present danger of a substantive evil; not subject to prior restraint; a permit may be required only for the use of a public place, not for the assembly itself. David et al. were committing no crime; the charges were "mere afterthought"; even the SolGen could not justify the arrests. De Jonge v. Oregon: "Peaceable assembly for lawful discussion cannot be made a crime."

paras.html: KMU / NAFLU-KMU (171483) — dispersal and arrests unwarranted. They were dispersed merely on Malacañang's directive cancelling all permits. The wholesale cancellation of permits disregards that "tolerance is the rule and limitation is the exception" and eliminated the distinction between protected and unprotected assemblies; respondents did not show the rallyists committed lawless violence. Under BP 880, LGUs regulate rallies and may revoke permits only after due notice and hearing on clear and present danger; petitioners learned of the revocation only at the dispersal, a fatal defect.

paras.text: Daily Tribune (171409) — illegal search and freedom of the press.

paras.html: Undisputed facts: warrantless search; seizure of materials for publication; done at about 1:00 a.m.; with only the building's security guard present; policemen stationed nearby; followed by official warnings. This violated Rule 126, Secs. 4 (probable cause, one specific offense), 8 (presence of the occupant or two witnesses), and 9 (daytime service).

paras.html: It also violated press freedom. Burgos v. Chief of Staff: padlocking newspapers is prior restraint. Though the Tribune was not padlocked, the seizure of materials, the stationing of policemen, and the "arrogant warning" to media are "plain censorship". The Tribune was targeted for its anti-government stance. The motto should be obsta principiis.

No. 5, violate citizens' rights, the Court must declare such acts unconstitutional and illegal.

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Petitions are partly granted. The Court rules that PP 1017 is CONSTITUTIONAL insofar as it constitutes a call by President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo on the AFP to prevent or suppress lawless violence. However, the provisions of PP 1017 commanding the AFP to enforce laws not related to lawless violence, as well as decrees promulgated by the President, are declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL. In addition, the provision in PP 1017 declaring national emergency under Section 17, Article VII [sic: Art. XII] of the Constitution is CONSTITUTIONAL, but such declaration does not authorize the President to take over privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest without prior legislation.

[This reading of "emergency" is narrower than the ponencia's.]

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to DISMISS ALL the petitions. The majority "has imprudently placed the Court in the business of defanging paper tigers" and ruled on non-justiciable issues based on fears that have not materialized. He agrees that PP 1017 is an exercise of the calling-out power and that declaring an emergency differs from exercising emergency powers.

paras.html: I. PP 1017 has no binding legal effect. Following his own ponencia in Sanlakas, a declaration like PP 1017 is "an utter superfluity" that only gives notice and is "devoid of any legal significance"; it cannot create or suspend rights. The calling-out power cannot vest new powers or authorize anyone to break the law; officers who commit illegal acts in its name may be held liable.

paras.html: The majority "grossly misreads" Sanlakas, which rooted the state-of-rebellion declaration in Secs. 1 and 18, Art. VII, not merely the Administrative Code. The calling out of the police derives from the Chief Executive and control powers, not the Commander-in-Chief clause, so the police may be directed to execute all laws. [sic: the opinion cites Sec. 17 for the Commander-in-Chief clause and Sec. 18 for control, apparently transposed.]

paras.html: Contrast with Marcos's PP 1081: it "placed" the country under martial law and ordered indefinite detention for a wide range of crimes; PP 1017 merely "declares." Calling them equivalent is "a rank insult" to martial-law victims.

paras.html: PP 1017 does not claim a power to issue decrees. Under noscitur a sociis, "laws and decrees" (separated by a comma from "orders and regulations promulgated by me") refers to existing Marcos decrees that still have the force of law. Striking the phrase is "killing a flea with dynamite when insect powder would do."

paras.html: PP 1017 is a valid exercise of inherent prerogatives of the President as head of state and "Chief Defender of the democratic way of life" (bully pulpit; Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation): it informs the people of an armed threat without suspending rights.

paras.html: II. Sec. 17, Art. XII. PP 1017 involved no actual takeover, so the discussion is obiter. He agrees that, as a general rule, takeover requires congressional approval (the provision does not say "by law," per Fr. Bernas; RA 6826 after the 1989 coup was enacted under Sec. 23(2), Art. VI). But the requirement is not absolute: in extreme situations where Congress cannot convene (e.g., bombs falling on Manila), the President may act, subject to judicial review. Araneta is inapplicable because it involved expired delegated powers.

paras.html: III. Vagueness is not limited to free speech cases. Citing his opinion in Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan, void-for-vagueness applies to penal statutes generally; overbreadth may be speech-only. The better ground is that PP 1017 creates no rights or obligations.

paras.html: IV. G.O. No. 5 has no infirmity. "Terrorism" has a widely accepted meaning covering acts already punishable under the RPC (rebellion, coup d'état, murder, arson). The majority's drinking-spree example applies equally to "lawless violence." Striking "terrorism" for vagueness after rejecting vagueness for PP 1017 is an inconsistency that "is breath-taking."

paras.html: V. The Court should not rule on individual grievances. Declaring the arrests and raid illegal makes the Court a trier of facts at first instance, without trial and without impleading the officers; it prejudges future cases and forecloses re-examining Umil v. Ramos (rebellion as a continuing crime). A declaration that PP 1017 cannot justify rights violations would suffice.

paras.html: The incumbent President is immune from suit during his tenure: the immunity need not be written in the 1987 Constitution or in law; the framers omitted it because it was "understood in present jurisprudence" (Bernas, 1986 ConCom; David v. Macapagal-Arroyo).
paras.text: The incumbent President is immune from suit during his tenure: the immunity need not be written in the 1987 Constitution or in law; the framers omitted it because it was "understood in present jurisprudence" (Bernas, 1986 ConCom; David v. Macapagal-Arroyo).

paras.html: The Philippine immunity is unqualified while he holds office: unlike the US rule, it does not distinguish whether or not the suit pertains to an official act, and it does not hinge on the nature of the suit; it covers a petition for the writ of habeas data, and no balancing of interests applies.
paras.text: The Philippine immunity is unqualified while he holds office: unlike the US rule, it does not distinguish whether or not the suit pertains to an official act, and it does not hinge on the nature of the suit; it covers a petition for the writ of habeas data, and no balancing of interests applies.

paras.html: It attaches to the office and need not be invoked: the Court may dismiss the suit even without the President invoking it. Immunity is not non-accountability: the remedy is to wait until his tenure (not term) ends by resignation or removal through impeachment.

paras.html: May 9, 2016: Davao City Mayor Rodrigo Roa Duterte was elected the 16th President. A key agenda of his administration was the relentless national crackdown on illegal drugs, which human rights advocates heavily criticized. Sen. De Lima was among the vocal critics.

paras.html: Sen. De Lima traces the President's personal animosity toward her to their first encounter, when he was Davao City Mayor and she was CHR Chairperson investigating the so-called "Davao Death Squad."

paras.text: The President is not immune because his statements were unlawful or made outside his official conduct; under Rodriguez v. Macapagal-Arroyo and Clinton v. Jones, immunity covers only the President's official acts.

paras.html: The statements violated RA 6713 and RA 9710, so they cannot be official acts worthy of immunity.

paras.html: Ruling on immunity is premature: the President has not invoked it in a verified return; immunity does not automatically attach every time he is sued, and only he may invoke it.

paras.html: In the US, a balancing of interests (private interest vs. intrusion on the Executive) comes first; under Clinton, separation of powers does not require staying all private suits until the President leaves office.

paras.html: The reason for immunity is absent: the suit will not degrade the office or harass or distract the President, especially since the OSG handles the suit; the attacks were personal, rooted in their CHR/Davao history.
paras.text: The reason for immunity is absent: the suit will not degrade the office or harass or distract the President, especially since the OSG handles the suit; the attacks were personal, rooted in their CHR/Davao history.

paras.html: Reply: immunity is not absolute; the cases cited for absoluteness (Forbes v. Chuoco Tiaco, Nixon v. Fitzgerald) predate the 1987 Constitution and are inconclusive on the incumbent's immunity. Direct resort to the SC was proper because the President has been collecting data on her and storing it in his office. As an aggrieved party, she deserves a judicial remedy.

paras.html: The immunity of the sitting President is absolute and extends to all suits, including amparo and habeas data petitions.
paras.text: The immunity of the sitting President is absolute and extends to all suits, including amparo and habeas data petitions.

paras.html: Despite its non-inclusion in the 1987 Constitution, the framers intended the immunity to attach to the incumbent [sic: decision says "Section 17, Article VII of the 1973 Constitution"; the immunity provision it later quotes is Sec. 15, Art. VII].
paras.text: Despite its non-inclusion in the 1987 Constitution, the framers intended the immunity to attach to the incumbent [sic: decision says "Section 17, Article VII of the 1973 Constitution"; the immunity provision it later quotes is Sec. 15, Art. VII].

paras.html: Under David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, the President is immune from any civil or criminal case during his tenure; impeachment is the way to hold him accountable. Absolute immunity rests on public policy, so stare decisis applies absent compelling reasons.

paras.html: This suit is the very distraction immunity prevents; the President is the sole embodiment of the Executive, unlike the collegial Judiciary and Congress.

paras.html: Lozada v. Macapagal-Arroyo: immunity attaches automatically to the office; the President need not invoke it. US cases are non-binding; Estrada v. Desierto cited Clinton and Fitzgerald only on the suability of a non-sitting President.

paras.html: Alternatively, even if immunity covers only official acts, the statements were made pursuant to the duty to faithfully execute the laws (Sec. 17, Art. VII): they revolved around her alleged involvement in the drug trade; mention of her relationship with Ronnie Dayan was incidental (intertwined with their alleged principal–accomplice relationship); and they were made while the HOR was investigating the drug trade in the National Penitentiary.

paras.html: Traced to Imperial Rome (Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis): princeps legibus solutus est (the emperor is not bound by statute) and quod principi placuit legis habet (what pleases the prince is law); revived in feudal Europe, especially England.

paras.html: Prof. Seidman: Roman, Church, customary, and feudal law fused into the maxim "the king can do no wrong," which has meant four things: (1) the King is literally above the law; (2) no remedy for royal wrongdoing through ordinary courts ("procedural" meaning); (3) the King has no capacity to do wrong (its true origin, Henry III being a minor); and (4) the King can do wrong but not lawfully.

paras.html: The US President can be served with judicial process: United States v. Burr (1807, Marshall, C.J.: subpoena duces tecum to Jefferson; the guard against vexatious subpoenas lies in the court's conduct after issuance); United States v. Nixon (1974: Nixon ordered to surrender the Watergate tapes; a general interest in confidentiality could not defeat the subpoena). But there is a dearth of precedent on suing an incumbent US President.

paras.html: By extent: absolute (actions within the scope of duties and discretionary, not ministerial; Butz v. Economou: only if essential to the conduct of public business → attaches to the function, not the office) vs. qualified (good-faith subjective test → Wood v. Strickland added the objective "should have known" test → Harlow v. Fitzgerald dropped the subjective test: (1) was the right clearly established at the time? (2) should the official reasonably have known the act was unlawful?).

paras.html: Courts cannot reverse the award of contest judges: "[T]he judiciary has no power to reverse the award of the board of judges of an oratorical contest." Neither would it interfere in literary contests, beauty contests, and similar competitions. Qualifier: this does not apply to activities the Government has chosen to regulate through the Games and Amusements Board (EO 392, s. 1950).

Neither would it interfere in literary contests, beauty contests, and similar competitions. Qualifier: this does not apply to activities the Government has chosen to regulate through the Games and Amusements Board (EO 392, s. 1950).

paras.html: No right to the prize before proclamation: A contestant has merely the privilege to compete, which does not ripen into a demandable right unless and until he or she is proclaimed winner by the appointed arbiters, referees, or judges.
paras.text: No right to the prize before proclamation: A contestant has merely the privilege to compete, which does not ripen into a demandable right unless and until he or she is proclaimed winner by the appointed arbiters, referees, or judges.

paras.html: Error is not wrong; damnum absque injuria: "Error and wrong do not mean the same thing." A "wrong" is the deprivation or violation of a right. If fraud or malice were proven, it would be a different proposition, but the action should then be against the individual judge or judges responsible, not the other judges.

paras.html: On March 12, 1950, a benefit inter-collegiate oratorical contest was held in Naga City. There were eight contestants, among them Nestor Nosce, Emma Imperial, and Luis General, Jr.

paras.html: Scoring system: Each judge was given a blank form on which he ranked the contestants from 1 (best) to 8. The ranks were added, and the contestant with the lowest sum got first prize, the next lowest second prize, and so on.

paras.html: Under "English," General was at first given 14, later increased to 15. paras.html: Judges should not assist or be detailed to the DOJ: The Court does not look with favor at the long-standing practice of judges being detailed in the Department of Justice to assist the Secretary, even if it were only in connection with his work of exercising administrative authority over the courts. The line between what a judge may and may not do with the other departments "must always be kept clear and jealously observed, lest the principle of separation of powers… be gradually eroded." No judge, even of the lowest court, should place himself where his actions on matters submitted to him would be subject to review, prior approval, or reversal by any authority other than the CA or the SC. The Court "feels very strongly that it is best that this practice is discontinued." [Stated in the body; the fallo only dismisses the complaint and furnishes the SecJ a copy.]

paras.html: He took his oath as CFI judge, station at Calamba, on June 29, 1970. His court was one of the 112 newly created CFI branches and had to be organized from scratch.

paras.html: After consultations, he accepted the Calamba municipal government's offer to supply space, the Laguna provincial government's promised financial help for supplies, and the national government's provision of equipment. Under Sec. 190 of the Revised Administrative Code, all these items must be furnished by the provincial government, but Laguna officials said the province could not do so.
paras.text: After consultations, he accepted the Calamba municipal government's offer to supply space, the Laguna provincial government's promised financial help for supplies, and the national government's provision of equipment. Under Sec. 190 of the Revised Administrative Code, all these items must be furnished by the provincial government, but Laguna officials said the province could not do so.

paras.html: Space: The Calamba mayor promised the west wing of the municipal building once the treasurer's office moved out, but the treasurer and several councilors objected. The mayor asked respondent to look for rental space, with the municipality paying. The Republic Bank negotiations failed when the owner refused to reduce the rent to ₱300 a month. The municipality finally leased the second floor of the Laguna Development Bank on October 26, 1970 after a month of negotiations; another month passed before funds were released to convert the hall into a courtroom and offices (including for the assistant provincial fiscal).

paras.html: Supplies and equipment: The provincial government appropriated ₱5,000 for supplies. In early December 1970, respondent ordered equipment from the DOJ Property Officer, but the appropriation for CFI equipment was released only on December 23, 1970, and procurement was still under way.

paras.html: Leave and DOJ assistance: Realizing it would be some time before he could preside, he applied for extended leave (in 16 years at the DOJ he had never taken extended leave and had forfeited leave benefits beyond the 10-month maximum). The Secretary of Justice prevailed upon him to forgo the leave and instead assist him, without being extended a formal detail, whenever he was not busy attending to his court's needs.

paras.html: Presidential immunity does not cover the acts of subordinates: A petition for prohibition against the DECS Secretary and Regional Director to stop a reassignment is not a suit against the President, because "the questioned acts are those of petitioners and not of the President." Furthermore, presidential decisions may be questioned before the courts where there is grave abuse of discretion or where the President acted without or in excess of jurisdiction (Medrana v. Office of the President).
paras.text: Presidential immunity does not cover the acts of subordinates: A petition for prohibition against the DECS Secretary and Regional Director to stop a reassignment is not a suit against the President, because "the questioned acts are those of petitioners and not of the President." Office of the President).

paras.html: Indefinite reassignment violates security of tenure: A reassignment with no fixed period and no stated objective or purpose from which its temporariness may be inferred is indefinite and violates the employee's security of tenure.
paras.text: Indefinite reassignment violates security of tenure: A reassignment with no fixed period and no stated objective or purpose from which its temporariness may be inferred is indefinite and violates the employee's security of tenure.

paras.html: Unconsented transfers (Bentain v. CA): Security of tenure covers "unconsented transfers which are tantamount to illegal removals." A temporary transfer without consent is permissible, but not when it is a preliminary step toward removal, a scheme to lure the employee away from his permanent position, designed to indirectly terminate his service, or meant to force his resignation.

COMELEC, 19 SCRA 1002; Brillantes v. Guevarra, 27 SCRA 138).

paras.html: Deportation power not limited to statutory grounds: The deportation of an undesirable alien may be effected (1) by the President, after due investigation, under Sec. 69 of the Revised Administrative Code, or (2) by the Commissioner of Immigration under Sec. 37 of the Immigration Law. Because Sec. 69 and EO 398 do not specify grounds, the Deportation Board may investigate an alien on a ground not enumerated in Sec. 37; the law grants the Chief Executive full discretion to determine whether an alien's residence is so undesirable as to injure the security, welfare, or interest of the State.

paras.html: Two modes of deportation. Under existing law, an undesirable alien may be deported:

paras.html: (1) by order of the President, after due investigation, under Sec. 69 of the Revised Administrative Code; and

paras.html: (2) by the Commissioner of Immigration, upon the Board of Commissioners' determination of the existence of the ground charged, under Sec. 37 of the Immigration Law, which specifies thirteen classes of deportable aliens (Po Siok Pin v. Vivo; Qua Chee Gan).

paras.html: Sec. 69 RAC requires only a prior investigation by the President or his authorized agent: the alien must be informed of the charges, given not less than three days to prepare his defense, and allowed to be heard by himself or counsel, to produce witnesses, and to cross-examine opposing witnesses.

paras.html: Inherent power. The State has the inherent power to deport undesirable aliens (Chuoco Tiaco v. Forbes, 228 U.S. 549). The Chief Executive may exercise it "when he deems such action necessary for the peace and domestic tranquility of the nation."
paras.text: Inherent power. The State has the inherent power to deport undesirable aliens (Chuoco Tiaco v. Forbes, 228 U.S. 549). The Chief Executive may exercise it "when he deems such action necessary for the peace and domestic tranquility of the nation."

paras.html: Citing J. Johnson's opinion in Forbes v. Chuoco Tiaco and Crossfield (16 Phil. 534): when the Chief Executive finds that an alien's continued presence is injurious to the public interest, "he may, even in the absence of express law, deport them" (also In re McCulloch Dick).

paras.html: "The right of a country to expel or deport aliens because their continued presence is detrimental to public welfare is absolute and unqualified" (Tiu Chun Hai and Go Tam v. Commissioner of Immigration).
paras.text: "The right of a country to expel or deport aliens because their continued presence is detrimental to public welfare is absolute and unqualified" (Tiu Chun Hai and Go Tam v. Commissioner of Immigration).

paras.html: No grounds specified. Sec. 69 and EO 398 (reorganizing the Board) do not specify the grounds for deportation. Par. 1(a) of EO 398 merely authorizes the Board, motu proprio or upon complaint, to investigate in the manner prescribed in Sec. 69 whether an alien is undesirable or not, and then to recommend deportation to the President.

Par. 1(a) of EO 398 merely authorizes the Board, motu proprio or upon complaint, to investigate in the manner prescribed in Sec. 69 whether an alien is undesirable or not, and then to recommend deportation to the President.

paras.html: Full discretion. As observed by J. Labrador (Tan Tong v. Deportation Board; Tan Sin v. Deportation Board), no legal or constitutional provision defines the power to deport, because the law intends to grant the Chief Executive "full discretion to determine whether an alien's residence in the country is so undesirable as to affect or injure the security, welfare or interest of the state." The adjudication of the facts also devolves on him, and his decision is final and executory.
paras.text: Full discretion. As observed by J. Labrador (Tan Tong v. Deportation Board; Tan Sin v. Deportation Board), no legal or constitutional provision defines the power to deport, because the law intends to grant the Chief Executive "full discretion to determine whether an alien's residence in the country is so undesirable as to affect or injure the security, welfare or interest of the state." The adjudication of the facts also devolves on him, and his decision is final and executory.

paras.html: Sole judge. The Chief Executive is the sole and exclusive judge of the existence of facts which warrant deportation, as disclosed in a Sec. 69 investigation; no other tribunal may reexamine or controvert the sufficiency of the evidence on which he acted (Martin v. Mott, cited in In re McCulloch Dick).

paras.text: Impeachable lawyer-officers cannot be disbarred during incumbency: "A public officer who under the Constitution is required to be a Member of the Philippine Bar as a qualification for the office held by him and who may be removed from office only by impeachment, cannot be charged with disbarment during the incumbency of such public officer."

paras.html: Nor criminally charged with offenses carrying removal: During incumbency, such officer cannot be charged criminally before the Sandiganbayan or any other court with any offense which carries with it the penalty of removal from office, or any penalty service of which would amount to removal from office.
paras.text: Nor criminally charged with offenses carrying removal: During incumbency, such officer cannot be charged criminally before the Sandiganbayan or any other court with any offense which carries with it the penalty of removal from office, or any penalty service of which would amount to removal from office.

paras.html: Not immunity, but a procedural requirement: The officer must first be removed by impeachment; only then may he be held to answer criminally or administratively (by disbarment). A fiscal or other prosecuting officer should forthwith and motu proprio dismiss charges against a Member of the Court; the remedy of one with a legitimate grievance is impeachment.

paras.html: Natural-born requirement for SC Members: "No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court ... unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines" (Sec. 7(1), Art. VIII). One who became a Filipino through his father's naturalization while a minor is a naturalized, not a natural-born, citizen. Until he proves otherwise in appropriate adversarial court proceedings and corrects his records, he cannot accept an appointment to the Court and may be enjoined from doing so.
paras.text: Natural-born requirement for SC Members: "No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court ... unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines" (Sec. 7(1), Art. VIII). One who became a Filipino through his father's naturalization while a minor is a naturalized, not a natural-born, citizen. Until he proves otherwise in appropriate adversarial court proceedings and corrects his records, he cannot accept an appointment to the Court and may be enjoined from doing so.

paras.html: Citizenship entries can be changed only judicially: a change in citizenship is a substantial change in the civil register; it requires a judicial order in an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding. Summary administrative correction under RA 9048 does not apply to nationality, and BI/DOJ recognition of natural-born status cannot amend a final naturalization decision.

paras.html: Specificity: An election protest must clearly and specifically allege, and then prove, the irregularities, specifying the precincts where each violation occurred and how it transpired. "When the protestant fails to meet the strict requirement of specificity and established rules on evidence to support the allegations of election irregularities, the election protest must be dismissed." (PET Rules, Rule 17(C)(d) and Rule 21.)
paras.text: Specificity: An election protest must clearly and specifically allege, and then prove, the irregularities, specifying the precincts where each violation occurred and how it transpired. "When the protestant fails to meet the strict requirement of specificity and established rules on evidence to support the allegations of election irregularities, the election protest must be dismissed." (PET Rules, Rule 17(C)(d) and Rule 21.)

paras.html: Pilot provinces (Rule 65): "In election protests before this Tribunal, the mandatory ceiling in designating pilot provinces is three. Failure to show substantial recovery of votes in these pilot provinces entails the protest's dismissal." The pilot provinces must cover all causes of action; if the protestant fails in them, the protest is dismissed forthwith "without further consideration of the other provinces mentioned in the protest," including a separate cause of action for annulment of elections.

paras.html: Annulment of election results vs. failure of elections: Electoral tribunals (including the PET) may annul election results as an incident of their judicial function and an indispensable consequence of their constitutional mandate, but only for the contested position and without special elections. The power to declare a failure of elections, and consequently to conduct special elections, "is lodged exclusively with the Commission on Elections." Both hinge on the same grounds and quantum of evidence.

paras.html: Protestant Ferdinand "Bongbong" R. Marcos, Jr. and protestee Maria Leonor "Leni" G. Robredo were two of six candidates for vice president in the May 9, 2016 national and local elections.
paras.text: Protestant Ferdinand "Bongbong" R. Marcos, Jr. and protestee Maria Leonor "Leni" G. Robredo were two of six candidates for vice president in the May 9, 2016 national and local elections.

paras.html: Robredo garnered 14,418,817 votes; Marcos garnered 14,155,344 votes, a slim margin of 263,473 votes.
paras.text: Robredo garnered 14,418,817 votes; Marcos garnered 14,155,344 votes, a slim margin of 263,473 votes.

paras.html: On May 30, 2016, Congress issued Resolution of Both Houses No. 1, which recognized the canvass results and proclaimed Robredo as the duly elected Vice President.

paras.html: The Protest and the Counter-Protest:
paras.text: The Protest and the Counter-Protest:

paras.html: On June 29, 2016, Marcos filed this Election Protest with the PET on two causes of action: (A) Robredo's proclamation is null and void because the Certificates of Canvass generated by the Consolidation and Canvass System are not authentic; and (B) massive electoral fraud, anomalies, and irregularities (terrorism, violence, intimidation, pre-shading of ballots, vote-buying, substitution of voters, flying voters, pre-loaded SD cards, misreading and improper rejection of ballots, malfunctioning VCMs, and abnormally high undervotes) in the protested precincts.

paras.html: The irregularities allegedly occurred in 39,221 clustered precincts in about 27 provinces and cities. Marcos prayed for annulment of elections in 2,756 clustered precincts and judicial revision in the remaining 36,465.

paras.html: July 12, 2016: The PET issued a Precautionary Protection Order directing COMELEC to safeguard the ballot boxes and election paraphernalia in the 92,509 clustered precincts covered by the Protest.
paras.text: July 12, 2016: The PET issued a Precautionary Protection Order directing COMELEC to safeguard the ballot boxes and election paraphernalia in the 92,509 clustered precincts covered by the Protest.

paras.html: Robredo filed a Verified Answer with Special and Affirmative Defenses and Counter-Protest. She argued that the Protest failed to specify the acts or omissions constituting fraud and that it was really a pre-proclamation controversy for the National Board of Canvassers. Her Counter-Protest contested 7,547 clustered precincts in 13 provinces (vote-buying, intimidation, substitution). She prayed for a preliminary hearing, dismissal for lack of jurisdiction and insufficiency, and affirmance of her proclamation.

paras.html: January 24, 2017 Resolution: The PET confirmed its jurisdiction under Art. VII, Sec. 4 ("sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the President or Vice-President"), found the Protest sufficient in form and substance, and denied Robredo's motion to dismiss and her request for a preliminary hearing on her affirmative defenses. Robredo moved for reconsideration (February 27, 2017); resolution was deferred until after the preliminary conference (June 6, 2017).

paras.html: First – Annulment of Proclamation: the COCs are not authentic and cannot be the basis of the vote count;

paras.html: Second – Revision and Recount: revision and recount of paper ballots and/or ballot images, and examination of voters' receipts, election returns, audit logs, voters' lists, VCMs, SD cards, etc., in all 36,465 protested clustered precincts (Rules 38–45, 2010 PET Rules);

paras.html: Third – Annulment of Elections: annulment of the vice-presidential results in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan for terrorism, intimidation, harassment of voters, and pre-shading of ballots in all 2,756 protested clustered precincts there.

paras.html: August 29, 2017 Resolution: The PET dismissed the first cause of action. The authenticity of the COCs could only be tested by a manual recount of all votes in all precincts, and since Marcos limited the recount to his second and third causes of action, resolving the first would have no practical effect. It also denied Robredo's motion for reconsideration and reiterated that the Protest was sufficient in form and substance.

Under Rule 65, Marcos designated Camarines Sur, Iloilo, and Negros Oriental as his pilot provinces; their results would determine whether the Tribunal would proceed with the rest. Witnesses were limited to three per clustered precinct, on pain of waiver. Action on the technical-examination motion was deferred as premature.

paras.html: COMELEC's Compliance: Eight petitions to declare failure of elections were filed in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao (none in Basilan); all were dismissed and the rulings became final; no special elections were held. COMELEC also stated that the PET can annul election results as an "indispensable consequence" of its mandate (applying *Abayon* by analogy), subject to the strictest standards and a more-than-50% threshold applied to all provinces, and that *Tan v. Hataman* was dismissed for mootness, not on the merits.

paras.html: The three vehicles for challenging election results are (1) failure of election cases; (2) pre-proclamation controversies; and (3) election contests (election protest or quo warranto). What remains consistent across all modalities is the requirement of specificity.

paras.html: Failure of elections (OEC Sec. 6) requires that the illegality affect more than 50% of the votes cast; the petition must specifically allege the essential grounds (*Pasandalan v. COMELEC*).

paras.html: Pre-proclamation controversies are limited to the exclusive list in OEC Sec. 243; under the AES, only the illegal composition or proceedings of the Board of Canvassers; they require "specific verbal objections subsequently reduced to writing" (*Macabago v. COMELEC*).

paras.html: An election protest is a contest between the defeated and winning candidates on grounds of fraud or irregularities in the casting and counting of ballots or preparation of returns; it centers on who validly obtained the plurality. Quo warranto questions election on grounds of disloyalty or ineligibility (*Samad v. COMELEC*; *Tecson v. COMELEC*).

paras.html: Rationale: "The power to annul an election should be exercised with the greatest care" (*Peña v. HRET*). Specificity deters fishing expeditions by losers "merely gambling with probabilities"; otherwise the process deteriorates into "an endless stream of crabs pulling at each other" (*Peña*). Practically, recounts demand significant time and resources.

paras.html: Rule 65, 2010 PET Rules: "The Tribunal may require the protestant or counter-protestant to indicate … the province or provinces numbering not more than three, best exemplifying the frauds or irregularities … If upon examination of such ballots and proof, and after making reasonable allowances, the Tribunal is convinced that … the protestant … will most probably fail to make out his case, the protest may forthwith be dismissed, without further consideration of the other provinces mentioned in the protest."

paras.html: The 1973 Constitution impliedly repealed RA 1793 by removing direct popular election of the president (giving it to the National Assembly); the vice-presidency was "constitutionally non-existent." BP 884 later constituted an independent PET (with a 12-month period). Under the 1987 Constitution, the PET became a constitutional institution; the SC's method of deciding contests through the PET "is actually a derivative of the exercise of the prerogative conferred" by Art. VII, Sec. 4, par. 7 (*Macalintal v. PET*).

Under the 1987 Constitution, the PET became a constitutional institution; the SC's method of deciding contests through the PET "is actually a derivative of the exercise of the prerogative conferred" by Art. VII, Sec. 4, par. 7 (*Macalintal v. PET*).

paras.html: Under Rule 67, 2010 PET Rules, the PET follows Art. VIII, Secs. 13–14 (consultation; stating facts and law) → no rule requiring decision within a particular timeframe, whether 20 or 12 months.

paras.html: The SC exercises judicial power only: "The Supreme Court and its members should not and cannot be required to exercise any power or to perform any trust or to assume any duty not pertaining to or connected with the administering of judicial functions."

paras.html: The SC as an entity ≠ its members: when the Organic Act speaks of the SC's "jurisdiction," it means the SC acting as a court, not its members sitting as a board of arbitrators. A board of arbitrators is not a "court" in any proper sense and possesses none of that jurisdiction.

paras.html: Arbitration cannot oust the courts of jurisdiction: courts should look with favor on arbitration unless the arrangement absolutely closes the doors of the courts; a law making the arbitrators' decision final against a public utility not a party to the franchise leaves it without recourse to the courts.

paras.html: Act No. 1446 granted a franchise to Charles M. Swift "to construct, maintain, and operate an electric railway, and to construct, maintain, and operate an electric light, heat, and power system from a point in the City of Manila in an easterly direction to the town of Pasig, in the Province of Rizal."

paras.html: Section 11 of the Act provides:
paras.text: Section 11 of the Act provides:

paras.html: "Whenever any franchise or right of way is granted to any other person or corporation, now or hereafter in existence, over portions of the lines and tracks of the grantee herein, the terms on which said other person or corporation shall use such right of way, and the compensation to be paid to the grantee herein by such other person or corporation for said use, shall be fixed by the members of the Supreme Court, sitting as a board of arbitrators, the decision of a majority of whom shall be final."

paras.html: Sec. 25, Art. XVIII requires recognition, not identical domestic processes: The VFA complies because it was concurred in by the Philippine Senate and recognized as a treaty by the US. That the US did not submit it to its Senate is a matter of internal US law. In addition, the presence of US troops under the VFA is "allowed under" the RP-US Mutual Defense Treaty, which both Senates ratified, because the VFA is merely an implementing agreement of the MDT.
paras.text: Sec. 25, Art. XVIII requires recognition, not identical domestic processes: The VFA complies because it was concurred in by the Philippine Senate and recognized as a treaty by the US. In addition, the presence of US troops under the VFA is "allowed under" the RP-US Mutual Defense Treaty, which both Senates ratified, because the VFA is merely an implementing agreement of the MDT.

paras.html: Immunity of visiting forces: The receiving State can exercise jurisdiction over a sending State's forces only to the extent agreed upon. Giving the US custody of an accused soldier during trial does not violate the Court's rule-making power or the equal protection clause.

paras.html: Custody versus detention: Custody during trial (Art. V, Sec. 6, VFA) differs from detention after conviction (Art. V, Sec. 10, VFA). Detention must be in agreed facilities and "by Philippine authorities"; detention in the US Embassy under US guard is not in accord with the VFA.

paras.html: Respondent L/CPL Daniel Smith is a member of the US Marine Corps. He was charged with rape under Art. 266-A of the RPC (as amended by RA 8353) together with S/Sgt. Chad Brian Carpentier, Dominic Duplantis, Keith Silkwood (all US Marines), and Timoteo L. Soriano, Jr. (the Filipino van driver), upon the sworn complaint of petitioner Suzette Nicolas.

Chad Brian Carpentier, Dominic Duplantis, Keith Silkwood (all US Marines), and Timoteo L. Soriano, Jr. (the Filipino van driver), upon the sworn complaint of petitioner Suzette Nicolas.

paras.html: The information alleged that on or about November 1, 2005, inside the Subic Bay Freeport Zone, Olongapo City, the accused, conspiring and by force, threat, and intimidation, with abuse of superior strength and taking advantage of the victim's intoxication, had carnal knowledge of Nicolas, a 22-year-old unmarried woman, inside a Starex van (Plate No. WKF-162) owned by Starways Travel and Tours and driven by Soriano.

paras.html: On December 4, 2006, the RTC of Makati convicted Smith of rape (Art. 266-A, par. 1[a], RPC) and sentenced him to reclusion perpetua, and ordered him to pay Nicolas ₱50,000 as compensatory damages and ₱50,000 as moral damages. Carpentier, Silkwood, and Duplantis were acquitted for insufficient evidence. [The fallo spells the name "Carpenter."]

Carpentier, Silkwood, and Duplantis were acquitted for insufficient evidence. [The fallo spells the name "Carpenter."]

paras.html: The RTC ordered that, under Art. V, par. 10 of the VFA, Smith serve his sentence in facilities to be agreed upon by Philippine and US authorities, and that pending such agreement he be temporarily committed to the Makati City Jail.

paras.html: Per the dissent of Puno, C.J.: Smith moved for reconsideration on December 5, 2006. On December 8, the public prosecutor manifested an agreement signed by Ambassador Kristie Kenney and Chief State Prosecutor Jovencito Zuno on transferring custody to the US Embassy; a similar agreement was later signed by Secretaries Gonzalez and Romulo. The RTC denied the MR on December 12, and Smith filed a petition for certiorari with a TRO prayer before the CA on December 14. The DFA intervened, and the SG adopted the DFA's position on December 28.

V, par. 6: custody of US personnel over whom the Philippines exercises jurisdiction "shall immediately reside with United States military authorities, if they so request," from the commission of the offense until completion of all judicial proceedings. paras.html: Examination of Medellin v. Texas:
paras.text: Examination of Medellin v. Texas:

paras.html: A Mexican national convicted of capital murder in Texas invoked the Vienna Convention and the ICJ's Avena judgment (and President Bush's Memorandum directing state courts to give it effect) to obtain a new trial. The US Supreme Court held that neither Avena nor the Memorandum is directly enforceable federal law.

The US Supreme Court held that neither Avena nor the Memorandum is directly enforceable federal law.

paras.html: Rule: a treaty may be an international commitment but is not binding domestic law unless Congress enacts implementing statutes or the treaty itself conveys an intention that it be self-executing and is ratified on that basis. Self-execution is determined by a textual approach; Art. 94 of the UN Charter ("undertakes to comply") is a commitment of the political branches, and the sole remedy (Security Council) is diplomatic.
paras.text: Rule: a treaty may be an international commitment but is not binding domestic law unless Congress enacts implementing statutes or the treaty itself conveys an intention that it be self-executing and is ratified on that basis. Self-execution is determined by a textual approach; Art. 94 of the UN Charter ("undertakes to comply") is a commitment of the political branches, and the sole remedy (Security Council) is diplomatic.

paras.html: The President cannot unilaterally make a non-self-executing treaty binding domestically; that responsibility falls to Congress (Youngstown framework).

paras.html: Implications of Medellin on the VFA:
paras.text: Implications of Medellin on the VFA:

paras.html: (1) The VFA's self-executing character must be clear from its text (a "clear statement requirement"); nothing in the VFA's text satisfies it.
paras.text: (1) The VFA's self-executing character must be clear from its text (a "clear statement requirement"); nothing in the VFA's text satisfies it.

paras.html: (2) Recognition by the US President through the former Ambassador is insufficient to make the VFA executory in the US. The VFA is a sole executive agreement: not one pursuant to a treaty (the MDT does not authorize the President to conclude implementing agreements), and not a congressional-executive agreement. It falls in Youngstown's third category, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb.
paras.text: (2) Recognition by the US President through the former Ambassador is insufficient to make the VFA executory in the US. The VFA is a sole executive agreement: not one pursuant to a treaty (the MDT does not authorize the President to conclude implementing agreements), and not a congressional-executive agreement. It falls in Youngstown's third category, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb.

paras.html: (3) A congressional act is necessary to transform the VFA's obligations into US domestic law; Bayan erred in holding it "inconsequential" whether the US treats the VFA as only an executive agreement, because binding effect internationally is distinct from domestic enforceability.
paras.text: (3) A congressional act is necessary to transform the VFA's obligations into US domestic law; Bayan erred in holding it "inconsequential" whether the US treats the VFA as only an executive agreement, because binding effect internationally is distinct from domestic enforceability.

paras.html: (4) There is an "asymmetry in the legal treatment" of the VFA: the Philippines enforced it (transferring Smith), while the US cannot enforce it domestically. The decisive mark of recognition as a treaty is whether the agreement has obligatory effects and may be a source of rights enforceable in the other State's domestic sphere.

paras.text: Under Medellin, the VFA is not US domestic law:

paras.html: Even a Senate-ratified treaty is not US domestic law without implementing legislation or self-executing terms; President Bush himself had to bow to this.
paras.text: Even a Senate-ratified treaty is not US domestic law without implementing legislation or self-executing terms; President Bush himself had to bow to this.

paras.html: The ICJ remedy is futile: the US withdrew its consent to compulsory ICJ jurisdiction in 1985; consent to jurisdiction is not consent to be bound; and enforcement through the Security Council is subject to the US veto. "It would be naïve and foolish" to implement as domestic law a treaty the US does not treat as its own domestic law.

paras.html: The US treats the VFA as a mere executive agreement:
paras.text: The US treats the VFA as a mere executive agreement:

paras.html: An executive agreement cannot alter existing law and must conform to statutes, while a ratified treaty can.
paras.text: An executive agreement cannot alter existing law and must conform to statutes, while a ratified treaty can.

paras.html: The Case-Zablocki Act merely requires notification to Congress of agreements "other than a treaty"; it does not enact them into domestic law. That the VFA was notified under it is "incontrovertible proof" that the US does not recognize it as a treaty. If a ratified treaty is not automatically domestic law, "with more reason" a merely notified executive agreement is not.

paras.html: Comm. Aquino objected that exempting judges' salaries violates the principle of uniformity of taxation and the equal protection clause; tax is levied on combined income, not on the salary, so why give justices special privileges?
paras.text: Comm. Aquino objected that exempting judges' salaries violates the principle of uniformity of taxation and the equal protection clause; tax is levied on combined income, not on the salary, so why give justices special privileges?

paras.html: Comm. Concepcion (sponsor) answered that the reason is judicial independence: taxing the salary is "an indirect way of decreasing their salary and affecting the independence of the judges." Aquino replied that respecting tenure is fine, but the special tax privilege still violates uniformity and equal protection.

paras.html: Comm. Ople shared the concern for judicial independence but warned that, in erecting a "bastion of justice," the Commission might end up with a "fortress of privileges, an island of extra territoriality"; the income tax exemption is "a kind of economic immunity" denied to the entire executive and legislative departments.

paras.html: Divisions may discipline lower-court judges: The first clause of Sec. 11, Art. VIII grants the disciplinary power to the Court en banc and lets it determine the procedure for exercising it; only the dismissal of a judge must be decided by the full Court. Under Bar Matter No. 209, the Court en banc decides cases where the penalty is dismissal, suspension of more than one year, a fine exceeding ₱10,000.00, or both; lesser penalties may be imposed by a Division.

paras.html: A Division's decision is the Supreme Court's decision: A decision of a Division, concurred in by a majority of the members who took part in the deliberations and voted, and in no case by fewer than three, is a decision of the Supreme Court (Sec. 4(3), Art. VIII; Circular No. 2-89).

paras.html: The error was "quite obvious" in light of PD No. 1, LOI No. 2, and PD No. 1275: the intent to abolish the Anti-Dummy Board "could not have been expressed more clearly" in LOI No. 2. Even if the City Fiscal failed to cite PD No. 1, a mere perusal of LOI No. 2 [sic: the printout reads "next of LOI No. 2"] would have shown that it was issued to implement PD No. 1.
paras.text: The error was "quite obvious" in light of PD No. 1, LOI No. 2, and PD No. 1275: the intent to abolish the Anti-Dummy Board "could not have been expressed more clearly" in LOI No. 2. paras.html: PDs issued by former President Marcos under his martial law powers have the same force as laws enacted by Congress (Aquino v. COMELEC, 62 SCRA 275 [1975]); LOI No. 2 is such an order, and neither PD No. 1 nor LOI No. 2 has been revoked or repealed.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy covers use and disposal of property: The grant of fiscal autonomy is more extensive than the mere automatic and regular release of approved appropriations; "real fiscal autonomy covers the grant to the Judiciary of the authority to use and dispose of its funds and properties at will, free from any outside control or interference."
paras.text: Fiscal autonomy covers use and disposal of property: The grant of fiscal autonomy is more extensive than the mere automatic and regular release of approved appropriations; "real fiscal autonomy covers the grant to the Judiciary of the authority to use and dispose of its funds and properties at will, free from any outside control or interference."

paras.html: COA audit power is qualified: COA's power to audit constitutional bodies with fiscal autonomy on a post-audit basis (Sec. 2(1), Art. IX-D) must be read in light of the Court's fiscal autonomy, the provisions on judicial independence, and jurisprudence. COA cannot substitute its own policy for the Court's on the disposal of the Court's property.

paras.html: Background: the retirement privilege

paras.html: By long-standing tradition, retiring Justices of the SC and the appellate courts purchase, for sentimental reasons, the government properties they used during their tenure. The practice is recognized as a privilege and a benefit, partly to reward long and faithful service.
paras.text: By long-standing tradition, retiring Justices of the SC and the appellate courts purchase, for sentimental reasons, the government properties they used during their tenure. The practice is recognized as a privilege and a benefit, partly to reward long and faithful service.

paras.html: On March 23, 2004, the Court En Banc issued a Resolution in A.M. No. 03-12-01 (Guidelines on the Purchase of Judiciary Properties by Retiring Members of the Supreme Court and Appellate Courts). Its whereas clauses rest the privilege on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy as defined in Bengzon v. Drilon and state that the privilege needs regulation so that respect for a retiring Justice's sentiments is consistent with restraint in disposing of government resources.

Electoral Commission: separation of powers obtains by actual division in the Constitution; each department has exclusive cognizance of matters within its jurisdiction and is supreme in its own sphere, but a system of checks and balances secures coordination, with the Judiciary as final arbiter determining the law.
