paras.html: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.
paras.text: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.

paras.html: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.
paras.text: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.

paras.html: Two concepts (citing Hood and Chan): decisional independence (a judge decides free from political or popular influence, based solely on the facts and the law) and institutional independence (the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive and Legislative; the collective independence of the Judiciary as a body).

paras.html: In re Macasaet (2008): individual judicial independence protects each judge's ability to decide with autonomy; institutional judicial independence protects judges as a class. A truly independent judiciary is possible only when both are preserved and public confidence in the Judiciary is maintained.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy is "one of the most important aspects of judicial independence." Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

paras.html: Although legislative control of the purse is generally unquestioned, any form of interference by the Legislative or the Executive on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy amounts to an improper check on a co-equal branch. To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.
paras.text: Although legislative control of the purse is generally unquestioned, any form of interference by the Legislative or the Executive on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy amounts to an improper check on a co-equal branch. To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.

paras.html: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.
paras.text: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.

paras.html: Bengzon v. Drilon (1992): fiscal autonomy is a guarantee of "full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it includes the power to levy, assess, and collect fees, fix compensation, and allocate and disburse funds. "Fiscal autonomy means freedom from outside control." If the SC says it needs 100 typewriters and DBM says only 10, autonomy becomes an "empty and illusory platitude."

paras.html: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.
paras.text: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy: Legal fees under Rule 141 fund the JDF and the SAJF. Any congressional exemption from legal fees necessarily reduces these funds and is "constitutionally infirm," because it impairs the Court's fiscal autonomy (Sec. 3, Art. VIII) and erodes its independence → the exemption of cooperatives under RA 6938, as amended by RA 9520, no longer stands.

paras.html: Art. 61, par. (6), RA 9520 (Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008) provides:
paras.text: Art. 61, par. (6), RA 9520 (Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008) provides:

paras.html: "(6) Cooperatives shall be exempt from the payment of all court and sheriff's fees payable to the Philippine Government for and in connection with all actions brought under this Code, or where such actions is brought by the Authority before the court, to enforce the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative."
paras.text: "(6) Cooperatives shall be exempt from the payment of all court and sheriff's fees payable to the Philippine Government for and in connection with all actions brought under this Code, or where such actions is brought by the Authority before the court, to enforce the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative."

paras.html: PHCCI claims this reiterates Sec. 62, par. 6, RA 6938 (Cooperative Code of the Philippines), which was the basis for the Court's own Resolution in A.M. No. 03-4-01-0 (15 July 2003) and OCA Circular No. 44-2007.

paras.html: The 2003 Resolution exempted cooperatives from court and sheriff's fees in actions under RA 6938, subject to guidelines: (a) the action is filed by the duly elected officers in the name of or on behalf of the cooperative; and (b) the action is filed under RA 6938 but limited only to enforcing the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative; otherwise, no exemption.

paras.html: The separation of powers has erected an "impregnable wall" keeping the rule-making power within the sole province of the Court. The other branches trespass on this prerogative if they enact laws or issue orders that effectively repeal, alter, or modify the Court's procedural rules → a legislative grant of exemption from legal fees (there, Sec. 39 of RA 8291) necessarily fails.

paras.html: Quo warranto lies against an impeachable officer on eligibility: Sec. 2, Art. XI "does not preclude a quo warranto action questioning an impeachable officer's qualifications to assume office." Lack of qualifications is not an impeachment ground; "Quo warranto, not impeachment, is the constitutional remedy prescribed to adjudicate and resolve questions relating to qualifications, eligibility and entitlement to public office."

paras.html: Prescription depends on who files: the one-year period under Sec. 11, Rule 66 still stands, but (1) a quo warranto filed by the State at its own instance through the SG is imprescriptible (not a blanket authority to file baseless actions); (2) one filed by the SG or a public prosecutor on relation of another, with leave of court, and (3) one filed by an individual in his or her own name are subject to it, except when established jurisprudential exceptions are present.

paras.html: Quo warranto (Rule 66) is a judicial determination of a person's right or title to a public office: eligibility or validity of the appointment. "[W]here the dispute is on the eligibility to perform the duties by the person sought to be ousted or disqualified a quo warranto is the proper action."

"[W]here the dispute is on the eligibility to perform the duties by the person sought to be ousted or disqualified a quo warranto is the proper action."

paras.html: Impeachment is a political process to determine whether the officer committed an impeachable offense (culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust). It does not ascertain eligibility or the legality of the assumption of office.

paras.html: Presidential immunity is personal to the President and may be waived: The privilege of immunity from suit "pertains to the President by virtue of the office and may be invoked only by the holder of the office; not by any other person in the President's behalf." An accused in a criminal case where the President is the complainant cannot raise it as a defense. Nothing in our laws prevents the President from waiving the privilege; the choice to exercise or waive it is solely the President's prerogative.

paras.html: Personal determination of probable cause (Sec. 2, Art. III): The Constitution requires the judge to personally satisfy himself of the existence of probable cause, not to personally examine the complainant and the witnesses. He may (1) personally evaluate the fiscal's report and supporting documents and issue the warrant on that basis; or (2) if he finds no probable cause on that basis, disregard the report and require supporting affidavits of witnesses.

paras.html: Following *Salonga v. Cruz Paño* (1985), the Court should not hesitate to quash a criminal prosecution in the interest of more enlightened and substantial justice where broader considerations of governmental power versus a preferred freedom are involved.

paras.html: The situation is unusual: the highest official, enjoying unprecedented public support, seeks the prosecution of a columnist, the publisher and chairman of the editorial board, the managing editor, and the business manager in "a not too indubitable a case" for libel. [sic: he refers to "four petitions"; three G.R. Nos. are consolidated.]

[sic: he refers to "four petitions"; three G.R. Nos. are consolidated.]

paras.html: He supports an all-out prosecution of a newspaperman who engages in unwarranted personal attacks or malicious distortions. But here the complainant is a powerful President who heads the investigation and prosecution service and appoints members of appellate courts.
paras.text: He supports an all-out prosecution of a newspaperman who engages in unwarranted personal attacks or malicious distortions. But here the complainant is a powerful President who heads the investigation and prosecution service and appoints members of appellate courts.

paras.html: Where harassment goes beyond the usual difficulties of an accused and makes media unwilling to criticize government, the SC, not a lower tribunal, should draw the line.

paras.html: *US v. Bustos* (1918): complete liberty to comment on public men; criticism is to be expected and borne for the common good.

paras.html: *People v. Perfecto* (1922): no official is so exalted that citizens must speak of him with bated breath; high office invites attacks rather than giving immunity from them.

paras.html: *Elizalde v. Gutierrez* (1977): a libel prosecution lacks justification if the words find sanctuary in the free press guaranty; it should not continue where there is likely to be a chilling effect on newspapermen, especially editors and publishers.

At trial, those safeguards "should be faithfully applied."
